schools.summary: Gill collects the guesses at Isaac's age, rejecting the five years of the Talmudists because a child could hardly have carried the wood, and running through thirteen, the twenty-five of Josephus and Bishop Usher, and the thirty-six of the Targum. Calvin reads after these things as covering the whole run of Abraham's trials rather than the last vision only, and sets them out: exile to his eightieth year, famine driving him into Egypt, his wife twice torn from his bosom, his nephew rescued at the peril of his own life, years of childlessness, and then the son obtained only to have Ishmael disinherited and driven off. Isaac alone remained, and Abraham was enjoying peace at home when God thundered suddenly out of heaven. On the trial itself he insists the wound was not chiefly paternal: set beside the conflict of conscience, the bereavement and the violence and even the father's being made executioner are mere shadows of conflicts, since the great source of grief was that in the person of this son the whole salvation of the world seemed to be extinguished. The contest was not with carnal passion but with piety itself, God as if engaging him in personal combat requiring the death of the boy to whose person he had himself annexed the hope of eternal salvation; so that the command was, in a certain sense, the destruction of faith, God shaking the faith the holy man had placed in his word by a counter assault of the word itself.

Henry puts the timing as the lesson it is: perhaps Abraham was beginning to think the storms had all blown over, and after all this encounter comes, sharper than any yet, for many former trials will not secure us from further ones, and we have not yet put off the harness. On the word he notes that some render it he did lift up Abraham, as a scholar who improves well is lifted up into a higher form, and states the distinction plainly, that God tempted him not to draw him to sin, as Satan tempts, but to discover his graces.

Clarke would avoid the English word altogether: though tempt, from tento, signifies no more than to prove or try, it is now generally used to imply a solicitation to evil, in which way God never tempts any man. He prefers what the versions do with it, the Greek having tried or pierced through, and Symmachus rendering it glorified, taking the root to mean glistering with light, whence a banner displayed — so that God put great honour on Abraham by giving him this opportunity of showing to all successive ages the efficacy of an unshaken faith. Wesley follows Henry's account of the trial almost word for word.

Ellicott describes the lull the command broke into: for twenty-five years the patriarch had wandered and seen the promise perpetually deferred without his faith failing, and now, at peace with his neighbours and with Isaac approaching manhood, everything seemed to presage a calm and happy old age. He finds the trial twofold, and puts the first half in a form the others do not reach. Human sacrifice was abhorrent to the nature of Jehovah, so Abraham's plain duty was to test the command, and no subjective proof would have served — had he been moved only by an internal impulse, his conduct would have deserved the same condemnation as the later Israelites who gave their firstborn in religious frenzy and got a deeper guilt for it. Only when he was satisfied that the command came from outside himself, and from the God he had so often conversed with, did the antecedents of his own life require obedience. He adds that the higher purpose was neither Abraham's good nor Isaac's but the instruction of the whole Church, since without its typical value a command seeming to authorise human sacrifice would be hard to reconcile to our consciences.

debates.question: In what sense did God tempt Abraham?

positions.position: not to draw him to sin, as Satan tempts, but to discover his graces — indeed to lift him up, as into a higher form
the English word misleads; the versions render it tried, or even glorified, so that the trial was an honour conferred
a severe test in which God assaulted the faith he had himself given, the command standing against the promise

outliers.note: makes Abraham's first duty the verification of the command rather than obedience to it, and distinguishes him from the child-sacrificing Israelites of later times precisely by that test

themes: the trial that came after all the others
in what sense God tempts
the word of God set against itself

2.pericope_label: Take now thy son, thine only son

schools.summary: Gill marks the exclusions the command begins with — not thine ox, nor thy sheep, nor thy ram, nor thy lamb, nor thy servant, but thy son. Calvin works the contradiction and unties it the same way Luther does. Abraham was commanded to cut in pieces the very charter of his salvation, since whatever favour he could hope for was bound up in the single promise that in Isaac shall thy seed be called, from which he necessarily inferred that his own salvation and that of the whole human race would perish unless Isaac remained. His mind must have been severely crushed when the command and the promise of God were conflicting within him; but having concluded that the God he had to do with could not be his adversary, he reconciled the two by hope without seeing how, and left the unknown issue to Providence — going, meanwhile, as with closed eyes, whither he was directed.

Clarke reports Warburton's observation that the order of the words gradually increases the sense and raises the passions higher and higher, and adds Jarchi's suggestion that the minuteness was meant to preclude any doubt about who was intended; he takes Moriah for the mountains of Jerusalem and passes on the conjecture that Abraham offered on the very mount where our Lord was afterwards crucified, noting that Beersheba lies some forty-two miles off, so that the party could not arrive until the third day. Wesley climbs the ladder rung by rung: not thy bullocks and thy lambs, which Abraham would willingly have parted with by thousands to redeem Isaac; not thy servant, no, not the steward of thine house; thy only son by Sarah, Ishmael being lately cast out, so that Isaac only was left — and must he go too? Yes: take Isaac, him by name, thy laughter, that son indeed.

Ellicott begins with the first word, which is not an adverb of time at all but an interjection of entreaty, ordinarily attached to requests to soften them, so that the sentence reads more as exhortation than command; and he sharpens the cruelty by comparison, since if childlessness had been unendurable to Abraham before, what must it be now, after so many years' enjoyment of a son and after giving up Ishmael for his sake. On the place he weighs the rival claim of Moreh in Sichem, urged by many able commentators and affirmed by the Samaritans, and rejects it on three grounds: Gerizim is far too remote from Beersheba to be reached early on the third day, since even the journey to Jerusalem takes twenty and a half hours; Moriah is described as a land, some part of which Abraham was to be shown; and Moreh was a place he had lived in and knew already. He also settles the sense of the command against Hengstenberg and others, who argued that Abraham was to surrender Isaac spiritually rather than slay him — a reading contradicted by the narrative itself and by the epistle, which locates the victory of his faith precisely in believing that though Isaac were killed the promise would still be fulfilled in him. Keil says the same from the other side, that the command was framed so that Abraham could understand it in no other way than as an outward burnt offering, and quotes Luther on the impasse: human reason would simply conclude either that the promise is a lie or that the command comes from the devil, since if Isaac must be killed the promise is void, and if the promise stands this cannot be God's command.

debates.question: Where was the land of Moriah?

positions.position: the mountains of Jerusalem, and probably the very mount where Christ was afterwards crucified
Moreh in Sichem, with the altar on Gerizim, as the Samaritans affirmed — rejected as too remote for a third-day arrival

debates.question: Was Abraham commanded to kill Isaac, or to surrender him spiritually?

positions.position: to kill him; the narrative and the epistle both forbid the softer reading
to kill him; no other form of words could have accomplished the complete surrender

outliers.note: states the logical impasse in Luther's words — promise or command, one of the two must be false — and answers that Abraham brought his reason into captivity to the obedience of faith rather than resolving it

themes: a command built to wound by degrees
where the land of Moriah lay
the promise and the command in contradiction

3.pericope_label: Abraham rose up early in the morning

schools.summary: Gill takes the command to have come in a dream or vision of the night, which is why the morning is the first moment Abraham could act on it. Calvin measures the obedience by the speed of it. Innumerable thoughts might have come into the holy man's mind, any one of which would have overwhelmed his spirit had he not fortified it by faith, and there is no doubt that Satan, during the darkness of that night, heaped upon him a vast mass of cares. To overcome them gradually by contending with them was heroical courage; but then immediately to gird himself to the command, and to rise early to do it, was a remarkable effort. Other men, prostrated by a message so dire, would have fainted and lain torpid as if deprived of life — and the first dawn was scarcely early enough for Abraham's haste.

Henry lists what Abraham had to break through, and the list is not gentle. The command seemed directly against an antecedent law of God forbidding murder — can the unchangeable God contradict himself, and can he who hates robbery for burnt offering delight in murder for it? It could not be squared with natural affection: cannot Abraham be obedient without being unnatural, and must the father of the faithful be the monster of all fathers? No reason was given, where a reason had been given when Ishmael was cast out; and Isaac was neither a martyr nor a ransom nor a criminal but a dutiful, obedient, hopeful son, so that one may ask what profit there is in his blood. It could not be squared with the promise. And afterwards there was Sarah to face, with the blood of Isaac staining his raiment, and the Egyptians and Canaanites and Perizzites to hear of it, to the eternal reproach of Abraham and his altars. What answered every one of these was simply that he was infallibly assured the command was God's and no delusion; God's commands are not to be disputed but obeyed. Henry also fills in two silences — Sarah was very probably told nothing, lest she prevent it, since there is so much in our own hearts to hinder our progress in duty that we have need to keep out of the way of other hindrances; and the servants were left at a distance lest they interpose and disturb so strange an oblation, as Christ, entering on his agony in the garden, took three disciples and left the rest behind.

Clarke adds what the Targum supplies where the text is silent, that the two young men were Eliezer and Ishmael, and the wood small wood, fig and palm, proper for a burnt offering. Wesley takes the rising as the first of the steps of obedience: he did not delay, did not demur, did not take time to deliberate, for those that do the will of God heartily will do it speedily, and while we delay time is lost and the heart hardened.

Ellicott thinks the minuteness of the preparations is itself the point — every step is recorded, as if to show the calmness with which Abraham girded himself for obedience. He took the wood ready cleft, not because there was none to be had on the spot, but so that when they arrived there should be nothing to distract their thoughts and they might proceed at once to the sacrifice.

outliers.note: puts into words the case Abraham could have made against the command — six distinct objections, from the law against murder to what the neighbouring nations would say — and lets the assurance that the voice was God's answer all of them at once

themes: objections a father might have raised
obedience measured by its speed
preparations made in advance

4.pericope_label: The third day, and the lamb for the burnt offering

schools.summary: Gill makes the three days do evidential work. Moriah lay some forty miles from Beersheba, so Abraham had travelled two full days, and all that while he had leisure to reconsider what he was about — and by proceeding after so much time to revolve it in his mind he shows he was satisfied that what he had heard was no illusion but an oracle of God, so that his obedience was neither rash nor hasty and his faith was sufficiently tried. Calvin calls Isaac's question a new instrument of torture, and does not doubt that God framed the boy's tongue to that appellation and directed him to that question, so that nothing might be wanting to the extreme severity of the grief. What he admires is how the knot is untied — by taking refuge in providence — and he turns it into a rule: whenever the Lord gives a command, many things occur to enfeeble our purpose, means fail, we are destitute of counsel, all avenues seem closed, and in such straits the only remedy against despondency is to leave the event to God, that he may open a way where there is none. On the promise to return with the lad he will not smooth things over: the words seem not free from dissimulation, and though some take them as prophecy, it may rather be that, trusting in providence, Abraham figured his son to himself as surviving even in death — and since he went as with closed eyes, there is nothing improbable in supposing that he spoke confusedly in a matter so obscure.

Clarke answers the same charge from the epistle, that Abraham accounted God able to raise him up even from the dead, and that it was as easy for God to restore his son after he had been a burnt offering as to have given him life in the beginning — he went therefore fully purposed to offer him, and confidently expecting to have him back. Of the exchange between father and son he says only that a paraphrase would spoil it, nothing being conceivable more tender than the question of the one and the reply of the other; and on the answer he hears prophecy, since all other lambs offered from the foundation of the world had been such as men chose and men offered, whereas this was the Lamb which God provided. Wesley turns the question on the reader: the fire is ready, that is the Spirit's assistance and God's acceptance, and the wood is ready, the instituted ordinances — but where is the lamb, and where is the heart?

Ellicott sets the two weary days of travel beside Hagar's in the wilderness, and marks the difference: hers were human sorrows only, while Abraham was giving up the son on whom his spiritual hopes depended. On seeing the place afar off he answers an objection drawn from the ground itself. The summit usually identified with Moriah cannot be seen from more than three miles away, which has been urged as proof that some more conspicuous hill must be meant; but afar off is used very indefinitely, and three miles agrees exactly with what Abraham did, since he left the servants there, laid the wood on Isaac, and walked the rest — and while three miles would sorely tax a boy carrying wood, from the point where Gerizim first becomes visible it would have been impossible. He adds that belief in the resurrection of the body was no novelty to Abraham, being part of the creed of both Chaldea and Egypt, and reads the answer about the lamb as meaning Isaac himself, so showing that the victim was not of Abraham's choosing but God's.

debates.question: Was Abraham speaking truthfully when he said he and the lad would return?

positions.position: yes, in faith — he expected Isaac to be restored to him even from the dead
the words are not free from dissimulation; more likely he spoke confusedly, going as with closed eyes in a matter so obscure

outliers.note: uses the three-mile sight-line of Moriah as a measurement rather than a difficulty, matching it against the distance a boy could carry wood and so ruling out the Gerizim identification

themes: three days to reconsider
the promise to return with the lad
God will provide himself a lamb

9.pericope_label: The altar built, and Isaac bound

schools.summary: Gill collects the traditions that gathered round the site: Maimonides reports it as a tradition in the hands of all that this is where David and Solomon built an altar in the threshing floor of Araunah, where Noah built one on coming out of the ark, where Cain and Abel offered, and where the first man offered when he was created and out of which he was made; the Mahometans put it at Meena, two or three miles from Mecca, and sacrifice their sheep there on that account. On the last moment he watches the hand go out, one would think in a trembling manner, for it is enough to make one tremble to think of it. Calvin reaches the same conclusion as the others about Isaac's consent — he was of middle age and might have been the stronger of the two, so force was not used against a struggling and unwilling youth, but he voluntarily surrendered himself, and can scarcely have done so unless he had already been told what the oracle required. Why bind a willing victim he answers practically: the holy man was anticipating a possible danger, lest something should happen in the middle of the act to interrupt it. And he admires the restraint of the telling, that the simplicity of the narrative of Moses is wonderful and has greater force than the most exaggerated tragical description, putting the sum of the whole in one line — that Abraham, when he had to slay his son, remained always like himself, his fortitude rendering that aged hand equal to a task the very sight of which was enough to destroy his whole body.

Clarke asks whether Isaac's character has been duly considered, or whether his excellence is lost in the supposition that he was too young to understand his danger and too feeble to resist. He puts his age at about thirty-three, the age at which his great Antitype was offered, and observes that even allowing the twenty-five of Josephus, it cannot be supposed that an old man of a hundred and twenty-five could have bound a young man in the prime of life without his consent — so that what prevailed here was not the superior strength of the father but the piety and filial obedience of the son. All of which he reads as typical: in both cases the father offers up his only-begotten son and himself binds him to the wood, in neither is the son forced to yield, and in neither is the life taken by the hand of violence. Wesley supplies what the text omits about the altar, an altar of earth, we may suppose, the saddest that ever was built, and reads the binding typologically — a sacrifice must be bound, and the great Sacrifice to be offered in the fulness of time must be bound, and therefore so must Isaac. He then breaks out of exposition into address: be astonished, O heavens, and wonder, O earth, for here is an act of faith and obedience that deserves to be a spectacle to God, angels and men, with Abraham's darling, the church's hope, the heir of promise, lying ready to bleed and die by his own father's hands.

Ellicott reports that the Jewish commentators agree the binding was done with Isaac's consent, nor could it well have been otherwise, so that his youthful faith was tried equally with his father's, his future life sanctified, and himself ennobled by being made a type of Christ. Keil describes the moment plainly, Isaac lying bound like a lamb upon the altar and about to receive the fatal stroke.

debates.question: Was Isaac able to resist, and did he consent?

positions.position: he was a grown man and could easily have resisted an old man of a hundred and twenty-five; what yielded was his filial obedience, not his strength
he was of middle age and perhaps the stronger; he surrendered voluntarily, and can scarcely have done so without knowing what the oracle required
the Jewish commentators agree he consented, nor could it well have been otherwise

outliers.note: praises Moses' plainness as more forcible than any heightened telling would have been, and reads the binding of a consenting victim as a precaution against interruption rather than against resistance

themes: the site and its accumulated traditions
whether Isaac consented
why a willing victim was bound

11.pericope_label: Lay not thine hand upon the lad

schools.summary: Gill takes the Angel for no created angel but the eternal one, the Son of God, and finds it clear from his swearing by himself and renewing the promise in his own name; he also guards the point that God never meant the boy actually to be slain, since he approves not of human sacrifices, and that the prevention was partly so that the thing might not be drawn into an example, though the Gentiles have imitated it notwithstanding. Calvin spots what the scene resembles and refuses the resemblance. The poets, when affairs are desperate in their fables, bring in some god who appears unexpectedly at the critical juncture; and it is possible that Satan, by figments of that kind, has laboured to obscure the wonderful interventions of God, so that the truth has not only been adulterated into a lie but distorted into material for fable, and made the more ridiculous. What actually happened is that in the very article of death God recalled Isaac from death to life and restored him to his father as one risen from the tomb. On the words now I know that thou fearest God he takes the difficulty head on: Augustine's way out, reading it as I have caused thee to know, he calls forced, but how can anything become known to God, to whom all things have always been present? The answer is condescension — God speaks of what he has proved by experiment as now made known to himself, not according to his own infinite wisdom but according to our infirmity. Nor were the earlier proofs insufficient in themselves; it is rather that when God willed him to proceed this far, the trial was at last complete, where in other persons a much lighter one would have sufficed. His own lesson is about the ceasing: it was not lawful for Abraham either to undertake or to relinquish anything except by God's authority, so let God prescribe to us our manner both of acting and of ceasing to act.

Henry marks the turn in the weather: hitherto the story has seemed to hasten toward a tragical end, and here the sky suddenly clears, the sun breaks out, and a bright and pleasant scene opens — the same hand that had wounded and cast down now heals and lifts up. He draws two rules from the timing, that our creature-comforts are likeliest to be continued to us when we are most willing to resign them to God's will, and that God's time to help his people is when they are brought to the greatest extremity, so that the nearer the danger is to execution, the more welcome the deliverance. On the divine knowledge he says briefly what Calvin says at length: God knew it before, but Abraham has now given a most memorable evidence of it and need do no more — and when God by his providence hinders the performance of our sincere intentions in his service, he graciously accepts the will for the deed.

Clarke explains why the hand was stayed at that particular moment by the typology he has been building. Since Isaac was to represent the real sacrifice, it was enough that in his own will and his father's the purpose of the immolation was complete: the father yields up the son, the son gives up his life, and on both sides, so far as will and purpose could go, the sacrifice was finished — God simply spares the father the torture of putting the knife to his son's throat. Wesley identifies the speaker with Henry as God himself, the eternal Word, the Angel of the covenant.

Ellicott notices something the others do not: that the narrative to this point had been Elohistic, and it is the angel of Jehovah who interferes to stop the sacrifice. Keil reads the interposition as showing that the sacrifice was already accomplished in Abraham's heart, so that he had fully satisfied the requirements of God and the outward fulfilment could be prevented.

debates.question: How can God say 'now I know' of what he must always have known?

positions.position: by condescension to human speech — God calls what he has proved by experiment a thing now made known to himself
God knew it before; what is new is the memorable evidence Abraham has given

outliers.note: guards the rescue against being read as a deus ex machina, arguing that Satan has turned such interventions into the stuff of fable precisely to make the real ones ridiculous

themes: the sky clearing at the last moment
how God can be said to learn
why the knife was stopped and not the command withdrawn

13.pericope_label: The ram in the thicket, and Jehovah-jireh

schools.summary: Gill notices the tense of the name, the future standing for the past, so that it records what God has just done and promises what he will do — as he provided a ram in the room of Isaac, so he has provided and will send his only Son. Calvin dismisses the rabbinic story that the ram had been created on the sixth day of the world as of a piece with the rest of their fictions, but does not doubt it was presented there by miracle, whether then first created or brought from elsewhere; and he keeps his own moral modest — since a ram is substituted, God shows us as in a glass the design of our mortification, that by the Spirit dwelling in us we, though dead, may yet be living sacrifices, more subtle allegories being available but resting, so far as he can see, on nothing. On the name he refuses to choose between the active and the passive and holds both. The change in process of time was deliberate and no mistake, and those who turned the active into a passive meant to teach that God not only looks upon his own but makes his help manifest to them, so that in turn he may be seen by them: the seeing has precedence, since by his secret providence he determines what is best for us, but the being seen hangs upon it, since he stretches out his hand and renders himself visible by experimental tokens.

Clarke gives the name literally as the Lord will see, whence the usual rendering that the Lord will provide, since his eye ever affects his heart and the wants he sees his hand is ready to supply; but he thinks the words were spoken prophetically, and prefers with Houbigant the Lord shall be seen, which the clause that follows seems to require — on this mount the Lord shall be seen — from which he infers that the sacrifice was understood to be representative, and that a tradition was kept up that Jehovah should be seen in a sacrificial way on that mountain. Wesley says it in the shorter form: the Lord will see, and will be seen in the mount, in the greatest perplexities of his people, for where God sees and provides, he should be seen and praised. He also notes that though the blessed Seed was now typified by Isaac, the offering of him was suspended till the latter end of the world, the sacrifice of beasts being accepted meanwhile as a pledge of that expiation — and that the temple was afterwards built on this same mount, with Calvary not far off.

Ellicott begins with the text: by a slight change in the shape of one consonant many ancient authorities read one ram rather than a ram behind, a correction he calls almost certain, since nowhere else is the word rendered behind used as an adverb of place; and the animal was probably the four-horned kind still common in the East. What he finds in the substitution is the doctrine itself — the ram took Isaac's place and by its actual death completed the typical representation, and there is no difficulty in the type being composed of two parts, what was wanting in Isaac supplied by the ram. Had Isaac actually died by his father's hand the possibility of a vicarious sacrifice would have been taught less clearly rather than more; so he rises again to life from the altar while the ram dies in his stead, and the two together set forth the whole mystery. On the proverb that grew from the name he sets the versions side by side, the Samaritan, Syriac and Vulgate reading in the mount Jehovah will provide, which changes none of the consonants but only the vowels added since the Christian era, while the Greek, without touching the vowels at all, has in the mount Jehovah shall be seen. He then asks the question none of the others do — when and how did the saying grow into a proverb, and who added the note? Possibly Moses, when he arranged these documents; less probably Ezra and the men of the Great Synagogue. Either way the proverb is a national testimony to the genuineness of the record, proving that the facts were so impressed on the memory of Abraham's descendants as to shape their thoughts and their language.

debates.question: Does Jehovah-jireh mean the Lord will provide, or the Lord shall be seen?

positions.position: the Lord shall be seen — the clause that follows requires it, and it was spoken prophetically of that mountain
both, and in order: God first sees to what is best for us, and then makes himself visible in the help he gives
the versions divide, the vowels being a later addition; the consonantal text supports 'will provide'

outliers.note: treats the proverb attached to the verse as evidence about the text's transmission — someone added the note, and the fact that the saying was current at all testifies to how deeply the event marked the national memory

themes: substitution and the vicarious sacrifice
the Lord will see, or the Lord shall be seen
how a name became a proverb

15.pericope_label: The oath, and the promise renewed

schools.summary: Gill reports Aben Ezra's judgment that this is a great oath which abides for ever, since God could swear by no greater than himself. Calvin sees a difficulty the others pass over. What had been promised freely before Isaac was born is here spoken of as a reward — because thou hast done this thing — and grace and reward are incompatible; since the blessing promised in the seed contains the hope of salvation, it might seem to follow that eternal life is given in return for good works, and the Papists boldly seize on the passage. His answer is to turn the argument round: if the promise was gratuitous before and is now ascribed to a reward, then whatever God grants to good works should be received as from grace; and if Abraham earned so great a compensation by his own virtue, the grace which anticipated him is made of none effect. What is freely given is yet called the reward of works — not to obscure the glory of God's goodness but to excite his people to the love of well-doing, when they perceive their acts of duty so far pleasing to him as to obtain a reward, while he pays nothing as a debt and merely gives his own benefits that title. The Lord shows himself doubly liberal, transferring to our works what properly belongs to his own pure beneficence. On possessing the gate of the enemies he adds the qualification he thinks indispensable, that the victory is promised not to Abraham's sons promiscuously but to Christ and his members so far as they adhere under one Head, since without some mark distinguishing the legitimate from the degenerate sons the promise would take in Ishmaelites and Idumeans equally with Israel.

Henry marks the escalation: the thing was said and sealed before, and now it is sworn; God interposed himself by an oath and, to speak with reverence, even pawned his own life and being upon it, that by all those immutable things his people might have strong consolation — if we exercise faith, God will encourage it, and if we improve the promises, God will ratify them. He counts four things in the blessing: the gift of the Spirit, the increase of the church, spiritual victories, and the incarnation, since in thy seed means one particular person and not many, as the apostle observes. And he states the balance carefully: Abraham's obedience is named as the consideration of the covenant, not that this was a proportionable consideration, but that God graciously put that honour upon what had honoured him.

Clarke supplies the human analogy, that an oath among men is an end to strife, and God, having no greater to swear by, swore by himself. On possessing the gate of the enemies he reads the gates broadly, as standing for all their strength, whether troops or counsels or fortified cities, and suspects our Lord had this very promise in view when he said the gates of hell should not prevail against his Church. Wesley lays the emphasis where the text does, on the clause because thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son.

Keil notes that Jehovah's swearing by himself never occurs again in his dealings with the patriarchs, and that later scripture keeps referring back to it — Luther held that everything said in the psalms about the oath given to David rests on this one, since in the promise those psalms are built on no oath is mentioned at all. Ellicott makes the same point as an argument: this is the sole instance of such an interposition in Holy Scripture, which plainly indicates that the trial was of no common kind and its typical teaching of no ordinary value. He also sums up what is new in this blessing as against those before it in three particulars — it is no longer a promise but a compact ratified by oath, it assures the seed of victory, and it transfers to Abraham's offspring the office of being the means of blessedness to all mankind.

debates.question: How can a promise given freely be spoken of here as a reward for obedience?

positions.position: because what is freely given may still be called the reward of works, to excite God's people to well-doing while he pays nothing as a debt
the obedience is named as the consideration of the covenant, though not a proportionable one — God putting honour on what had honoured him

outliers.note: traces the later scriptural appeals to this oath, and passes on Luther's observation that the psalms about God's oath to David rest on this passage, since the promise to David records no oath of its own

themes: an oath sworn once and never repeated
a free promise called a reward
possessing the gate of the enemies

19.pericope_label: The return to Beersheba, and the family of Nahor

schools.summary: Gill notices an absence: Isaac is not mentioned in the return, though there is no doubt he came back with his father, since we hear of him in the house afterwards, and the Targum of Jonathan's account — that the angels took him to the school of Shem the great, where he stayed three years — cannot be depended on. On the names he takes Huz for the founder of the land of Uz where Job dwelt and Buz for the father of the Buzites, Elihu's family, and reports the common view that the Chaldees sprang from Chesed, while noting the difficulty, that the Chaldees are mentioned before this man was born unless they are so named by anticipation. Calvin reads the quiet at Beersheba as part of the story rather than a coda: this notice is inserted, along with what follows about the increase of Abraham's kindred, to show that the holy man, brought up again from the abyss of death, was made happy in more ways than one, God so reviving him that he should be like a new man. He explains that Moses records the progeny of Nahor because Isaac was to take his wife from it, the mention of women in scripture being rare, so that of the many daughters credibly born to Nahor one only is introduced here; and he explains the concubine's sons being listed apart as occupying a less honourable place, refusing to let the custom justify itself — that it entered Nahor's mind to take a second wife does not make polygamy lawful, but only shows he supposed lawful for himself what had really sprung from the worst corruption.

Henry finds two reasons for the genealogy standing here. It shows that though Abraham saw his own family dignified with peculiar privileges, admitted into covenant and blessed with the entail of the promise, he did not look upon his relations with contempt or disdain, but was glad to hear of the increase and prosperity of their households; and it makes way for the story of Isaac's marriage to Rebekah, a daughter of that family.

Clarke says the notice is introduced solely to prepare the reader for what comes next, and to show that providence was preparing, in one of the branches of Abraham's family, a suitable spouse for his son; on the names he adds the Greek reading that makes Kemuel father of the Syrians, and identifies Huz with Uz in Arabia Deserta, the country of Job. Wesley follows Henry's two reasons closely.

Ellicott adds the human circumstance, that dwelling so far apart Abraham would seldom have news of those he had left at Haran, and that besides the domestic interest the knowledge was probably what decided him to seek a wife for his son among his own kindred. On the names he denies the identifications the others accept: Kemuel was not the progenitor of the Aramaic race but the ancestor of the family of Ram to which Elihu belonged, and Chesed was not the ancestor of the ancient Chaldees but possibly of the small tribe of robbers of the same name who plundered Job — of the rest, no trace remains in history. He also notices a pattern and refuses to build on it: Nahor has twelve sons, eight by his wife and four by his concubine, as Jacob has twelve by two wives and two concubines, and Ishmael twelve; the coincidences are curious but afford no ground for calling the narratives mythical, since coincidences quite as strange are found in every history and in daily life. Keil observes that with the sacrifice of Isaac the test of Abraham's faith was complete and the purpose of his calling answered, so that the history of his life now hastens to its termination, and the account of Nahor's family is introduced at just this point.
